Field surveys of the Mud darter (Etheostoma asprigene) in the Cache River drainage have provided detailed growth records for this small benthic darter. Hatchlings emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs with a minute neonate wet weight of 0.00063 grams [Wwb = 0.00063 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of slightly over one millimeter. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae remain largely lecithotrophic for several days, absorbing endogenous reserves before commencing first exogenous feeding. Young-of-the-year individuals grow steadily through their first summer, and by the onset of winter many attain a standard length near the size associated with the onset of gonadal differentiation. The average standard length at puberty, determined through histological examination of gonad tissue in field-collected specimens, is 3.2 centimeters [Lp = 3.2 centimeters]. This threshold marks the transition from a strictly somatic growth phase to the earliest stages of reproductive capability, although actual spawning is typically deferred until the following spring.

For populations inhabiting the Mississippi embayment, longevity records have been compiled from otolith annuli of known-age individuals maintained under controlled laboratory conditions. At a constant water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for the Mud darter is 1095 days [am = 1095 days], a duration consistent with the relatively short life cycles typical of small-bodied, iteroparous percids. This figure represents the time from egg fertilization to natural death in the absence of predation or disease, and it places Etheostoma asprigene among the shorter-lived members of its genus. Comparative data for related species such as Etheostoma caeruleum suggest somewhat longer potential longevities in larger-bodied congeners, but the Mud darter's abbreviated lifespan likely reflects its high metabolic demands and early reproductive schedule under warmwater stream conditions. The 21 °C regime used in these studies corresponds to typical late-spring and summer stream temperatures within the species' native range.

Under the same thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the time since birth at puberty for Mud darter males and females combined is 365 days [tp = 365 days]. This one-year interval corresponds to attainment of the 3.2 centimeter size threshold, and it indicates that most individuals born in a given spawning season become reproductively active during the following breeding period. Field observations confirm that first-year fish are generally absent from spawning aggregations in early spring but appear in gravid condition by late spring, consistent with the laboratory-derived estimate. The synchrony between the time since birth at puberty (365 days since birth) [tp = 365 days since birth] and the annual temperature cycle is likely an adaptive feature aligning this milestone with the onset of spring spawning conditions in this species at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C].

Body size at the conclusion of the growth trajectory has been assessed from large series of museum specimens spanning multiple decades and localities across the species' range. The ultimate standard length attained by Mud darter is 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters], a value that represents the typical maximum for adults in robust condition. This asymptotic length is comparatively modest even among darters, reflecting the species' preference for shallow, slow-moving stream habitats where prey availability may limit maximal size. Sexual dimorphism in ultimate length is minimal, with both sexes reaching similar maximum sizes, although gravid females occasionally exhibit slightly greater standard lengths due to distension from egg masses. The 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters] figure is consistent across most populations examined, suggesting a conserved genetic ceiling on somatic growth in this taxon.

Corresponding to this length maximum, the ultimate wet weight of adult Mud darters has been modeled from length-weight relationships calibrated with fresh specimens. The predicted adult body mass at the asymptotic length is 1.7 grams [Wwi = 1.7 grams], a modest value that underscores the species' allocation strategy toward early reproduction rather than continued somatic expansion. This mass is achieved only by individuals that survive beyond their first reproductive season and enjoy favorable foraging conditions through multiple growing periods. Comparisons with other darters of similar body plan, such as the closely related Etheostoma gracile, reveal that the Mud darter's ultimate wet weight (1.7 grams) [Wwi = 1.7 grams] is typical for its size class, although slight geographic variation exists, with specimens from nutrient-rich deltaic streams averaging marginally heavier masses than those from upland tributaries.
